questions.stem: Claude summarized a 30-page vendor contract you attached and wrote: 'The contract auto-renews for 24 months unless cancelled 90 days before expiry.' This line is going into an email to your director. What is the most efficient way to check it?

options.a: Ask Claude to quote the exact clause and give its section number, then read that clause in the contract yourself
options.b: Ask Claude whether it's sure
options.c: Regenerate the summary and see whether the line comes back the same
options.d: Send it as is, because the contract was attached

questions.explanation: A grounded claim can point to its evidence, so asking for the clause and reading it yourself is fast and conclusive ({a}). Asking for reassurance ({b}) gets a fluent answer either way. Consistency across regenerations ({c}) doesn't prove accuracy. An attached source ({d}) lowers the risk of errors without removing it, and this line describes a contract commitment.

questions.stem: Claude drafted a job ad for a software engineer that uses phrases like 'young, energetic team' and 'digital native.' What is the issue, and what should you do?

options.a: The wording signals an age preference, which can discourage qualified applicants and create legal risk; ask for inclusive wording and check it against your hiring policy
options.b: The tone is too casual for a job ad; ask for a formal rewrite
options.c: The ad is too long; ask for a shorter version
options.d: Nothing; these phrases are standard in job ads

questions.explanation: Evaluating output covers bias as well as factual errors, and age-coded language in a job ad is a real fairness and compliance problem ({a}). {b} and {c} change the style and keep the biased phrases. {d} confuses a common phrase with an acceptable one.

questions.stem: Claude built a pricing comparison table with totals calculated from 40 line items you pasted in. The table is going into a client proposal. What validation is needed?

options.a: Recompute the totals independently, for example in a spreadsheet, before the proposal goes out
options.b: Ask Claude to double-check its math in the same chat
options.c: Nothing, because you supplied the numbers
options.d: Round the totals so small differences don't matter

questions.explanation: Precise arithmetic over many figures is a weak fit to accept unchecked, and a client-facing proposal makes the numbers consequential, so they get verified independently ({a}). The same process checking itself ({b}) isn't an independent check. Correct inputs ({c}) don't guarantee correct sums. Rounding ({d}) hides errors.

questions.stem: Claude wrote a market summary with no sources attached. Which TWO details are hallucination red flags? (Select TWO)

options.a: 'According to a 2025 McKinsey survey, 73% of retailers plan to...' with no link or attached source
options.b: A precise figure for next quarter's market size, stated as fact
options.c: A general explanation of what market share means
options.d: A suggestion to verify the figures before publishing
options.e: A note that Claude can't see your internal sales data

questions.explanation: A named study with a precise statistic and no source ({a}), and a confident, specific figure about the future ({b}), fit the red-flag profile: precision and authority without grounding. A general definition ({c}) is low risk, and {d} and {e} are signs of honest, calibrated output.

questions.stem: Claude summarized a customer interview and wrote: 'The customer is frustrated with onboarding and plans to cancel.' The transcript mentions onboarding friction but says nothing about cancelling. What is the problem?

options.a: An unsupported inference is presented as fact; edit the line to what the transcript supports, or label it clearly as an interpretation
options.b: Nothing; it's a reasonable reading of the frustration
options.c: The summary is too short
options.d: The summary needs a more formal tone

questions.explanation: Details beyond the source are a hallucination red flag, and a cancellation claim could trigger real business decisions, so the output has to match its evidence ({a}). A plausible reading ({b}) still isn't supported by the transcript. {c} and {d} are style issues.

questions.stem: Research mode returns a summary of a new data regulation with eight cited sources. Your compliance team will base a plan on it. Which TWO steps are needed before anyone uses it? (Select TWO)

options.a: Open the cited sources and confirm that each key claim matches what the source says, and that the sources are current and authoritative
options.b: Have the compliance owner review the conclusions before the plan is built on them
options.c: Nothing; the citations prove the summary is accurate
options.d: Run research mode again and keep the claims that appear twice
options.e: Ask Claude to rate the reliability of each source

questions.explanation: Citations make claims checkable, which helps only if someone checks them ({a}), and regulatory content goes through a qualified reviewer ({b}). Citations alone ({c}) don't prove the summary represents its sources correctly. Repeated claims ({d}) show consistency, which isn't accuracy. Claude grading its own sources ({e}) is no independent check.

questions.stem: Your manager wants to roll Claude out to all 200 employees next week for every kind of task. What do you recommend?

options.a: Pilot one or two well-defined workflows with a small group, measure before and after (time spent, error rate), then expand
options.b: Roll it out to everyone at once to build momentum
options.c: Wait until AI tools stop making mistakes
options.d: Let each employee figure it out without guidance

questions.explanation: A measured pilot shows the real value and the limits on a small scale before the whole company depends on it ({a}). A big-bang rollout ({b}) spreads untested habits everywhere at once. {c} waits for something that won't happen. {d} produces uneven quality and no evidence.

questions.stem: Which TWO tasks are strong fits for Claude in a marketing team's workflow? (Select TWO)

options.a: Drafting five subject-line variants for an A/B test
options.b: Turning a webinar transcript into a blog draft and three social posts
options.c: Deciding which agency gets a $200,000 contract
options.d: Reconciling 5,000 ad-spend transactions with no independent check
options.e: Reporting a competitor's announcement from yesterday, from memory

questions.explanation: Drafting variants ({a}) and repurposing content across channels ({b}) are classic strong fits, with a person reviewing the output. A spending decision ({c}) needs human accountability, precise reconciliation at volume ({d}) belongs in a spreadsheet or finance system, and yesterday's news ({e}) is beyond the model's knowledge unless research mode grounds it.

questions.stem: You're presenting a Claude pilot to leadership. Which framing is most appropriate?

options.a: 'Meeting summaries now take 10 minutes instead of 45. The meeting owner still reviews each one, because outputs can contain errors.'
options.b: 'Claude eliminates errors from our summaries.'
options.c: 'Claude will replace the operations team.'
options.d: 'The benefits can't really be measured.'

questions.explanation: Good stakeholder communication pairs a concrete, measured benefit with an honest limitation ({a}). {b} promises something no probabilistic system delivers. {c} overstates the role and invites resistance. {d} gives leadership nothing to decide with.

questions.stem: A colleague opens Claude and types 'help me with the Q3 board deck.' The results are unfocused. What should be defined before prompting?

options.a: The deliverable, the audience, the source material and what a good result looks like
options.b: Which model to use
options.c: Nothing; Claude should infer it
options.d: The slide color scheme

questions.explanation: Solution design starts from the task: what you need, for whom, from which sources, and how you'll judge it ({a}). Model choice ({b}) comes later and won't rescue an undefined task. Claude can't infer goals nobody has stated ({c}). Colors ({d}) are a detail of the deliverable.

questions.stem: A legal team handles NDAs in five steps: intake, first-pass review against the team's playbook, negotiation, approval and signature. Where does Claude add the most value with the right safeguards?

options.a: First-pass review: compare each NDA to the playbook and flag deviations for a lawyer to decide on
options.b: Final approval
options.c: Signing on the company's behalf
options.d: Negotiating directly with the other party, unsupervised

questions.explanation: Claude fits the draft-and-analyze stage, with a qualified person keeping the decision ({a}). Approval ({b}), signature ({c}) and unsupervised negotiation ({d}) would put legal accountability on a tool.

questions.stem: You want Claude to summarize an internal incident report that contains customers' names and email addresses. Your company's AI policy allows internal documents and prohibits customer personal data. What do you do?

options.a: Remove or anonymize the customer details first (the summary doesn't need them), then summarize
options.b: Paste it in, because it's an internal document
options.c: Use the most capable model so the data stays safe
options.d: Paste it in and ask Claude to ignore the names

questions.explanation: Check the policy before pasting: the report is allowed, the customer data isn't, and the task works without it ({a}). Being internal ({b}) doesn't change the personal-data rule. Model choice ({c}) has nothing to do with data handling. Asking Claude to ignore data ({d}) comes after you've already shared it.

questions.stem: A sales rep wants to upload a prospect's RFP, marked confidential, so Claude can help draft the response. Your AI policy says nothing about third-party confidential documents. What is the best action?

options.a: Ask the policy owner or legal before uploading, and treat the document as sensitive until there's an answer
options.b: Upload it, since the policy doesn't forbid it
options.c: Upload only the pages that look less sensitive
options.d: Rewrite the RFP from memory and upload that

questions.explanation: When the policy doesn't cover a case, escalate to the policy owner and stay on the cautious side in the meantime ({a}). Silence in the policy ({b}) doesn't amount to approval. Partial uploads ({c}) and paraphrasing from memory ({d}) still share confidential content, and the rewrite adds errors.

questions.stem: Your organization requires disclosure when AI helps produce external content. You drafted a customer newsletter with Claude and then edited it heavily. What applies?

options.a: Follow the disclosure rule as written, because your edits don't change how the draft was produced
options.b: Skip disclosure, because your edits make it your own work
options.c: Disclose only if a customer asks
options.d: Describe the newsletter as written and fact-checked without AI

questions.explanation: Transparency rules apply as written ({a}). Editing ({b}) doesn't remove the requirement, disclosure on request ({c}) isn't what the policy says, and {d} misrepresents how the work was made.

questions.stem: Which TWO uses make Claude the decision-maker in a situation where a qualified person must own the call? (Select TWO)

options.a: Using Claude's ranking alone to decide which employees are laid off
options.b: Sending Claude's answer about a customer's legal rights to the customer without legal review
options.c: Drafting three versions of an internal FAQ for a manager to choose from
options.d: Brainstorming names for a team offsite

questions.explanation: Decisions that affect people's livelihoods ({a}) or legal standing ({b}) need a qualified human to own them, however good the draft looks. {c}, {d} and {e} are drafting and organizing work where a person still chooses what to use.

questions.stem: A financial advisory firm uses Claude to draft client emails that explain investment options. Which control is essential?

options.a: Compliance review of client-facing investment content before it's sent, including a check of every figure
options.b: Using the most capable model
options.c: A disclaimer at the bottom of every email, with no review
options.d: Sending the drafts faster to improve service

questions.explanation: Investment explanations are regulated advice, so qualified review comes before sending ({a}). A stronger model ({b}) doesn't change who is accountable. A disclaimer ({c}) can't replace the review that regulation requires. Speed ({d}) is beside the point.

questions.stem: Your prompt 'Write an email about the new expense tool' produced something generic. Which TWO additions would improve it most? (Select TWO)

options.a: Who the email is for and what it should get them to do
options.b: The tool's key facts, attached or pasted in: launch date, how to get access, where to get help
options.c: 'Make it amazing'
options.d: A request for ten versions
options.e: A switch to the most capable model

questions.explanation: Generic output comes from missing context, and the audience and goal ({a}) and the source material ({b}) are two of the five parts of a complete business prompt. Enthusiasm ({c}) adds no information. More versions ({d}) of an underspecified email are more generic emails. A stronger model ({e}) still can't know facts you didn't give it.

questions.stem: You need a 20-page market analysis with competitor profiles, a pricing comparison and recommendations. One big prompt produced a shallow result. What is the best approach?

options.a: Break it into steps: agree on an outline, draft each section from its sources, then do a final pass for consistency and tone
options.b: Ask for 'much more detail'
options.c: Rewrite the single prompt with every requirement in capitals
options.d: Regenerate until a deeper version appears

questions.explanation: Multi-part deliverables work better as a sequence of smaller steps you can check ({a}). {b} and {c} keep the one-giant-prompt problem. {d} is regenerate-and-hope.

questions.stem: Claude's first draft of a customer apology is too long and too formal. Which follow-up works best?

options.a: 'Cut this to about 120 words, make the tone warmer and more direct, keep the refund details, and apologize in the first sentence.'
options.b: 'Make it better.'
options.c: Regenerate the response
options.d: Start a new chat with the same prompt

questions.explanation: Specific feedback gives Claude concrete changes to make ({a}). {b} gives it nothing to act on, and {c} and {d} roll the dice again on an unchanged request.

questions.stem: You want campaign ideas for a product launch. Which prompting strategy fits brainstorming?

options.a: Ask for many varied ideas first (say, 20 across different angles), then evaluate and narrow them with your criteria in a follow-up
options.b: Ask for the single best idea
options.c: Ask for ideas with final budgets attached
options.d: Give no context, so Claude is unconstrained

questions.explanation: Brainstorming works best as volume and variety first, then judgment ({a}). Asking for one best idea ({b}) skips the exploration. Budgets ({c}) belong to a later planning step. With no context ({d}), the ideas won't fit your product or audience.

questions.stem: You need a project timeline that you'll revise with Claude over several rounds and then share with your team. Which output format fits?

options.a: An Artifact: a standalone deliverable in its own panel that you can refine and share
options.b: A plain chat reply you copy out each time
options.c: Research mode
options.d: A screenshot of the chat

questions.explanation: Artifacts are made for standalone deliverables you'll iterate on and share ({a}). Chat replies ({b}) suit quick answers. Research mode ({c}) finds current sources. A screenshot ({d}) can't be edited.

questions.stem: Which TWO tasks justify Opus over Sonnet? (Select TWO)

options.a: A strategy recommendation that synthesizes six long reports, where an error would be expensive
options.b: Working out how obligations interact across five related contracts before a high-stakes negotiation
options.c: Reformatting a list of 30 names into a table
options.d: Writing a two-line reply to a colleague

questions.explanation: Opus is for complex, high-stakes reasoning across a lot of material ({a}, {b}). Sonnet is the everyday default, and quick, simple tasks like {c}, {d} and {e} suit Sonnet or Haiku.

questions.stem: You need to sort 400 short customer comments into five well-defined themes today. Speed matters more than nuance. Which approach fits?

options.a: Haiku with the five themes clearly defined, followed by a spot-check of a sample
options.b: Opus for maximum quality on every comment
options.c: Research mode
options.d: One comment per chat, so each gets full attention

questions.explanation: Quick, well-defined tasks at volume are Haiku's case, and a sample check keeps the quality honest ({a}). Opus ({b}) spends time and cost on a task that doesn't need deep reasoning. Research mode ({c}) searches for current sources, which this task doesn't need. {d} wastes hours.

questions.stem: A long chat about a proposal has become slow, and Claude has started mixing up details from early drafts with the current version. What is the best move?

options.a: Start a new chat with a short summary of the current decisions and the latest draft, and keep reference documents in Project knowledge
options.b: Keep going and correct each mistake as it appears
options.c: Paste the entire chat history into a new chat
options.d: Switch to Haiku for speed

questions.explanation: Restart, summarize and persist is the fix for an overloaded chat: a fresh context with only what matters ({a}). {b} keeps the overload, {c} moves it to a new chat, and {d} changes speed without fixing the mix-ups.

questions.stem: In a team Project, where should each of these go: (1) 'Always write in British English and use our headline format'; (2) the 40-page brand guidelines PDF; (3) the brief for this week's campaign?

options.a: (1) Project instructions, (2) Project knowledge, (3) the chat prompt
options.b: (1) Project knowledge, (2) Project instructions, (3) Project instructions
options.c: (1) The chat prompt, (2) the chat prompt, (3) Project knowledge
options.d: (1) Project instructions, (2) the chat prompt, (3) Project knowledge

questions.explanation: Standing rules go in instructions, reference documents go in knowledge, and details for one task go in the chat ({a}). {b} swaps rules and documents and makes a one-week brief permanent. {c} retypes standing rules every time. {d} re-uploads the guidelines in every chat and stores a temporary brief permanently.

questions.stem: Your weekly report draws on a Google Doc of sales notes that the team updates daily. You've been uploading a copy every Monday, and sometimes it's out of date. What is the better setup?

options.a: Connect Google Drive so Claude reads the current version of the document
options.b: Upload a copy twice a week
options.c: Paste the notes from memory
options.d: Copy the notes into the Project instructions

questions.explanation: Connectors suit material that lives in another tool and changes often, so Claude reads the current version ({a}). More frequent uploads ({b}) shrink the gap without closing it. Memory ({c}) adds errors. Instructions ({d}) hold standing rules, and pasted notes there go stale just as fast.

questions.stem: A Project keeps quoting last year's prices. Both the 2025 and the 2026 price sheets are in Project knowledge. What fixes this?

options.a: Remove or replace the outdated price sheet, and if both must stay, state in the instructions which one is current
options.b: Correct Claude in every chat
options.c: Switch to Opus
options.d: Use research mode for prices

questions.explanation: Stale knowledge produces confidently outdated answers, so the fix is maintaining the knowledge itself ({a}). Correcting every chat ({b}) never ends. A stronger model ({c}) still reads both sheets. Your prices are internal, so searching for them ({d}) won't find the right ones.

questions.stem: You asked for 'a table comparing vendors,' and each time the columns come out different. What is the most effective fix?

options.a: Show the exact structure: list the columns in order, or paste a sample row, and ask Claude to follow it
options.b: Regenerate until the columns match
options.c: Switch to Opus
options.d: Ask for 'a better table'

questions.explanation: A wrong format every time means the format was described vaguely, and a concrete example fixes that ({a}). {b} is regenerate-and-hope, {c} changes the model without clarifying the request, and {d} is still vague.

questions.stem: Claude answered a question about your company's travel reimbursement limits using general industry norms. The real policy is a PDF on the shared drive. What is the best fix?

options.a: Attach the policy (or add it to Project knowledge) and ask Claude to answer from it, quoting the relevant section
options.b: Ask the same question again with more emphasis
options.c: Switch to Opus
options.d: Tell Claude its answer is wrong and ask it to try again

questions.explanation: Confident but wrong claims about your own business come from missing source material, so give Claude the policy and ask for the quote ({a}). Emphasis ({b}) and a stronger model ({c}) can't produce a policy Claude hasn't seen. Telling Claude it's wrong ({d}) without the policy gets you a different guess.

questions.stem: On Monday you changed a Project's instructions, switched the model and uploaded new knowledge files. Since then, the outputs are worse. What should you do?

options.a: Roll back, then reapply one change at a time and compare the results on the same test inputs
options.b: Change everything again
options.c: Ask Claude what went wrong
options.d: Delete the Project and start over

questions.explanation: With three changes at once, you can't tell which one hurt quality, so change one variable at a time against the same inputs ({a}). {b} adds more confusion, {c} asks Claude to explain configuration changes it can't observe, and {d} throws away a setup that worked before Monday.
